content:
I was pointed at https://www.cs.ru.nl/~freek/fta/xindex.html from a discussion on the nForum, an example of what today would be called Blueprint-driven formalisation, but done more by hand, and in Coq, from 2000:

The project consisted of three phases:

  1. Writing in LaTeX a detailed account of the Kneser proof in ordinary mathematical style
  2. Writing in Coq the steps of the Kneser proof but as axioms, so without any Coq proofs: a so-called theory development
  3. "Filling in" the Coq proofs in this theory development, leading to a proof development

Obviously it is easy to arrive at this type of approach when one wants to seriously attack formalisation: Landau's Foundations of Analysis being formalised in AUTOMATH in the late 70s is something like this, but the informal-but-detailed proof document was created independently, not as part of the process of formalisation. Having a concrete example stated as such with a record of it, and the outputs as they were at the time, is I think less common.

Does anyone know of similar older records? I haven't dug into @Freek Wiedijk 's website to find more, there might be earlier examples lurking there.

I don't have anything older to contribute. However, this brings to mind a recent (in historical terms) effort of Doron Zeilberger to do what I call crowdsourcing for referees: he took a result to be vetted, broke it into some number of pieces (between 50 and 100?) and farmed off the pieces to various reviewers, the idea being that each piece was small enough for a reviewer to verify/refute quickly. It was the first time I saw someone "blueprint" or divide a paper in that way for processing. I think similar examples should be considered attempts at formalization, even if they were not to be fed into a mechanical machine.
sender_full_name: J. J. Issai (project started by GRP)
